armenians: Seljuk invasions in the 11th century pushed Armenian armies to add composite bowmen as an answer to large mounted forces, and the Armenian Composite Bowman ignores the armor of its target. The same upheaval drove many Armenians to Cilicia on the Mediterranean coast, where their new kingdom kept a fleet, and the Cilician Fleet technology gives their Galleys and Dromons extra range.
aztecs: Garland Wars, the technology that gives Aztec infantry +4 attack, is named after the ritual battles the Aztecs arranged in peacetime to test their warriors' courage and take captives for sacrifice. Warriors in those fights carried wooden clubs made to stun and maim, adding obsidian blades only when they meant to kill. The Jaguar Warrior is named after one of the elite warrior orders of Aztec society.
bengalis: Battle chariots had fallen out of use in most of the Indian subcontinent, yet the Pala emperors of Bengal still fielded them, and the Ratha brings one back as a unit that switches between bow and melee. Mahayana Buddhism flourished under the same emperors, which fits the Mahayana technology: it makes Bengali Villagers and Monks take up less population space.
berbers: The Genitour carries an adarga, the apple-shaped leather shield made chiefly in Fes and used by the light cavalry of Muslim Spain, and the same shield is the Berber civilization icon. The unit's name goes back, through the Spanish jinete, to the Zenata, a Berber people whose horsemen were famous in Iberia. Teammates of a Berber player can train Genitours at their own Archery Ranges from the Castle Age.
bohemians: Jan Hus was executed in 1415 for preaching church reform, and the Hussite Wars that followed run through this civilization. Hussite Reforms replaces the gold cost of Monks and Monastery technologies with food, and the Hussite Wagon recalls the fortified wagons armed with artillery that Jan Zizka and Prokop the Great turned against the Imperial armies.
britons: The Longbowman recalls the early battles of the Hundred Years' War, when English longbowmen cut down ornately armored French knights from long range, and every Briton foot archer apart from the Skirmisher gains range in the Castle and Imperial Ages. Warwolf, the technology that gives Trebuchets blast damage, is named after the huge trebuchet Edward I had built for the siege of Stirling Castle in 1304.
bulgarians: When a Konnik's horse dies, the rider gets up and keeps fighting on foot. That fits the two peoples who made medieval Bulgaria: Slavic settlers who fielded light infantry, and Bulgar horsemen from Central Asia, whose heavily armored cavalry stayed the backbone of the Bulgarian army and was among the most feared in Europe.
burgundians: With Burgundian Vineyards researched, Farmers slowly earn gold as well as food. Medieval Burgundy's monasteries were centers of learning and winemaking, a tradition the region keeps to this day. Flemish Revolution turns every Villager into anti-cavalry Flemish Militia, which fits the restless cities of Flanders, whose townsmen beat an army of French knights at the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302.
burmese: Bagan, capital of the Pagan kingdom, held more than 10,000 temples, pagodas and monasteries between the 11th and 13th centuries, and Burmese Monastery technologies cost half as much. War elephants were the elite of the Pagan army and often carried a howdah, a carriage for several archers, which gives its name to the technology that adds armor to Burmese Battle Elephants.
byzantines: Every Age adds hit points to Byzantine buildings, walls and Farms, much as the walls of Constantinople let the eastern empire outlast the western one by about a thousand years. Greek Fire, the unique technology for Fire Ships and Dromons, is named after the Byzantine secret weapon that was sprayed from a hose and devastated an Arab fleet in the eighth century, though nobody knows what it was made of.
celts: Mostly based on the Gaels of Scotland and Ireland, the Celts are the civilization you play in the William Wallace tutorial campaign. With the Stronghold technology their Castles heal nearby infantry, and they can take enemy sheep and other herdable animals even when enemy units stand right next to them.
chinese: Gunpowder was invented in China, yet the Chinese have no Hand Cannoneer or Bombard Cannon, because the civilization is loosely based on the Song dynasty, when gunpowder still came in early forms such as fire lances and rockets. The Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart take their place, and the Rocketry technology makes Lou Chuan warships fire rockets that deal area damage.
cumans: Two Turkic peoples, the Cumans and the Kipchaks, merged on the Kazakh steppe, and their horsemen often ended up fighting for others: Cuman cavalry helped the Bulgarians drive out the Byzantines in 1185, and Cuman-Kipchak slaves sold in Egypt became Mamluks, who later seized power there. Cuman Mercenaries fits that history by letting teammates train five free Elite Kipchaks per Castle.
dravidians: Southern India made wootz, an early form of steel that traveled the trade routes to the Middle East and became known there as Damascus steel, and the Dravidian technology Wootz Steel lets infantry and cavalry attacks ignore armor. The Urumi Swordsman carries another local weapon, the urumi from Kerala, a flexible blade swung like a whip.
ethiopians: The Shotel Warrior carries the curved sword that the game's history text calls the most characteristic Ethiopian weapon, used to drag riders off their horses or to reach around shields. Royal Heirs fits that purpose, since it reduces the damage Shotels and Ethiopian camel units take from mounted enemies.
franks: Charles Martel turned the Franks into a cavalry army in the 8th century, and in 732 his horsemen beat the Muslim invaders coming north from Spain at Poitiers, so it fits that Frankish mounted units get 20% more hit points from the Feudal Age. The unique unit, the Throwing Axeman, hurls the francisca, the throwing axe named after the Franks themselves.
georgians: Medieval Georgia held out among the mountains south of the Caucasus, where its armies used the terrain to strike back at invaders, and Georgian units and buildings take less damage when they fight from higher ground. The Svan Towers technology takes its name from the defensive towers of Svaneti and lets Georgian towers fire arrows that pass through several targets.
goths: Stone Walls are missing from the Goth tech tree, and an Ensemble Studios design document from 1998 traces this to Totila, the Ostrogothic king who tore down the walls of the cities he captured during the Gothic War. That forced the Byzantines to fight in the open field, where the Goths had the numbers, and in the game the Goths play the same way, with masses of cheap infantry.
gurjaras: Shrivamsha Riders are named after a horse breed known for its speed and endurance, which sources describe in the cavalry of the Pratihara king Mihira Bhoja, and in the game they dodge incoming projectiles. Gurjara Mills can also be filled with sheep and other herdables that produce food, one of several economic bonuses the developers drew from the farming wealth of Gujarat.
hindustanis: Ghaznavid and Ghorid armies relied on ghulams, former slaves trained as professional soldiers, who came to dominate battlefields and palaces alike. The Hindustani Ghulam is an armored infantryman whose spear passes through several enemies. Grand Trunk Road, which speeds up all gold income, is named after the highway across northern India that Sher Shah Suri rebuilt in the 16th century.
huns: Hunnic players never need Houses, since the population cap starts at its maximum, and that suits a people who moved west with their families and great herds of horses in search of new grassland. Their Tarkans, horsemen who excel at tearing down buildings, recall the raids of Attila, whose army sacked most of the towns of what is now northern France before its defeat at Châlons.
inca: Conquered peoples filled the ranks of the Inca army, each fighting with its own weapons, so one imperial force could include Andean slingers and Cañari spearmen under Inca officers. The civilization's Slinger and long-speared Kamayuk fit that picture. From the Castle Age, Inca Villagers also benefit from the infantry upgrades at the Blacksmith, so they can fight off raiders themselves.
italians: Late medieval Italian armies were generally made up of and led by condottieri, professional mercenaries who served whoever paid the most. The Condottiero unit fights with bonus attack against gunpowder units, and like a true hired sword it works for allies too, who can train Condottieri at their own Barracks.
japanese: Samurai means "those who serve": warrior retainers whose code put loyalty to their lord first, roughly the Japanese counterpart of the European knight. The Samurai unit does bonus damage against unique units, which makes it the Japanese answer to other civilizations' elite troops. Kataparuto, the technology that makes Trebuchets pack, unpack and fire faster, is the Japanese way of saying "catapult".
jurchens: Hunting mattered so much to the Jurchens that every man was expected to join the group hunts, and in the game the meat of their hunted animals and livestock never decays. Their Thunderclap Bombs technology, which makes Grenadiers and Rocket Carts explode when they die, is named after the explosive weapon the Jurchen Jin dynasty used against the Mongols at the siege of Kaifeng in 1232.
khitans: Instead of tilling Farms, Khitan Villagers raise herds on Pastures, which fits a pastoral people from east of the Khingan Mountains whose economy depended on cattle and horses. Their Mounted Trebuchet comes from the neighboring Tanguts, whose Boxi regiment rode camels that carried small catapults or staff slings on their backs.
khmer: War elephants of the Khmer Empire sometimes carried ballistae, and the Ballista Elephant puts one on the battlefield as the civilization's unique unit. Khmer Villagers can also hide inside Houses when raiders come, and the Khmer need no particular buildings to advance in Age, a rule no other civilization in Age of Empires II shares.
koreans: Admiral Yi Sun-sin used armored, cannon-carrying turtle ships to defeat the Japanese fleets after the invasion of 1592, and the Korean Turtle Ship is a slow, heavily armored warship that fires cannonballs. Shinkichon is named after the singijeon, the Korean rocket arrows fired from hwacha carts, and it gives Rocket Carts and Turtle Ships extra range and more rockets.
lithuanians: Grand Duke Gediminas secured Lithuania's borders with a network of hillforts held by professional guards and by the Leiciai, his personal servants, and both appear in the game: Hill Forts gives Town Centers extra range, and the Leitis is a horseman whose attack ignores armor. Lithuanian Knights and Leitis also grow stronger for every Relic stored in a Monastery.
magyars: Hungarian raiders of the 9th and 10th centuries were mostly light cavalry armed with Asian recurve bows from their steppe past, and the civilization gets both: Recurve Bow for its mounted archers and the Magyar Huszar, whose name gave Europe the word hussar. Corvinian Army, named after King Matthias Corvinus, swaps the Huszar's gold cost for extra food.
malay: The great maritime empires of the archipelago, such as Srivijaya and Majapahit, are known as thalassocracies, and the Thalassocracy technology upgrades Malay Docks into Harbors that shoot several arrows at once. The Karambit Warrior is named after the karambit, a small curved blade popular with Javanese peasants, and he takes up only half a population space.
malians: After his pilgrimage to Mecca, Mansa Musa had the Sankore and Djinguereber madrasas built in Timbuktu, and the Malian team bonus makes Universities work 80% faster. The pilgrimage itself drew attention everywhere for the camels loaded with gold that traveled with him, and gold runs through the civilization too: Malian Villagers drop off 10% more of it.
mapuche: Lautaro, a Mapuche taken by the Spanish as a boy, escaped knowing how they fought with cavalry, and in 1553 the Mapuche used horsemen for the first time to win the Battle of Tucapel. The Bolas Rider throws the bolas, a hunting tool of weighted stones on a cord that snared enemies, and in the game its hits slow the target down.
maya: Designer Sandy Petersen came up with the bonus that makes Maya resources last 15% longer because he wanted this economic civilization to have something long-lasting and unique, and it became his second favorite creation after the Huns not needing Houses. Real Maya warriors preferred slings and javelins, and Hul'che Javelineers reflects that by letting Skirmishers throw an extra projectile.
mongols: Once the Nomads technology is researched, Mongol Houses keep their population space even after they are destroyed, and Drill makes Siege Workshop units move 50% faster, which helps them keep pace with the horse archers. The Mongols also appear in the campaigns of more expansions than any other civilization.
muisca: Fallen Guecha warriors were mummified and carried into battle by other soldiers, who believed the dead gave their bearers strength and ferocity, and in the game a dying Guecha Warrior heals the Guecha Warriors around it. The Muisca are also the people behind the El Dorado legend, which grew out of a ritual in which a new chieftain was covered in gold dust and taken out onto Lake Guatavita.
persians: Parthian Tactics arrives for the Persians a full Age early, a nod to the Parthian shot, first recorded at the Battle of Carrhae and carried on by the Sasanian Empire into the early Middle Ages. Their heavy cavalry ends in the Savar, which replaced the Paladin after the developers decided that a European style knight did not fit the civilization.
poles: A folwark was a manor farm worked by serfs, and estates like it made the Polish nobility rich as farm exports grew in the late Middle Ages. In the game every Mill becomes a Folwark that takes a share of the food from nearby Farms. The nobles appear too: Szlachta Privileges, named after the Polish nobility, cuts the gold cost of the Knight line by 60%.
portuguese: Prince Henrique, better known in English as Henry the Navigator, oversaw the development of the caravel, a light and fast ship, and sponsored many expeditions to Africa. The Caravel is the Portuguese unique warship, and the Feitoria, named after the trading posts of the Portuguese Empire, slowly generates resources on its own in exchange for 20 population.
romans: By 395 the Western Roman army could no longer guard every border at once, so it held the frontier with a token force and kept an elite mobile reserve ready for any breakthrough. Those field troops were the comitatenses, and the Roman technology named after them trains Militia-line units, Knights and Centurions 50% faster and gives them a charge attack.
saracens: The Mameluke takes its name from the mamluks, slave soldiers of high status who seized power in Egypt in 1250 and stopped the Mongols ten years later; in the game it is a camel rider with a short ranged melee attack. Bimaristan, named after the hospitals of the medieval Islamic world, lets Saracen Monks heal several nearby units at once.
shu: Zhuge Liang, the strategist who served Liu Bei, is credited with inventing a crossbow that shot several bolts at once. Shu archery builds on that: the War Chariot fires from a large repeating crossbow, and Bolt Magazine gives it and the Archer line extra projectiles. The White Feather Guard is named after the elite infantry that protected Liu Bei in his war against Wu.
sicilians: Norman adventurers first came to southern Italy as mercenaries and ended up ruling it, and they guarded their lands with formidable keeps called donjons. Sicilian Serjeants build those Donjons in place of the usual towers, and the First Crusade technology, named after the expedition that made the Norman Bohemond ruler of Antioch, calls up a band of five Serjeants from each Town Center.
slavs: In the Rus' principalities the boyars, landowning aristocrats who also led the armies, held the power of their rulers in check, and the Slav unique unit is a heavily armored Boyar on horseback. Druzhina, named after a prince's armed retinue, gives infantry splash damage. Detinets lets Castles and towers be built partly with wood, which fits the timber fortresses the Rus' built before they turned to white stone.
spanish: Supremacy turns Spanish Villagers into fighters with +6 attack, +2/+2 armor and +40 hit points. The Conquistador, a gunpowder horseman, and the Missionary, a Monk on horseback, belong to the conquest of the Americas that began after 1492, the year Granada fell and Columbus reached the New World under Queen Isabel's patronage.
tatars: During his invasion of India in 1398, Timur is said to have sent camels loaded with burning straw against the war elephants of the Delhi Sultanate. The Flaming Camel recalls that story: it explodes like a Petard and does bonus damage to elephants and mounted units. The Keshik is named after the bodyguard of the Great Khan and earns gold every time it strikes.
teutons: A crusading order of German warriors gave the Teutonic Knight its name; the real order spread Christianity into the Baltic by conquest until Alexander Nevsky stopped it on frozen Lake Peipus. That religious background fits their Monks, who heal from twice the usual range, and a team bonus that makes units and buildings harder to convert.
tupi: Blackwood was the usual material for Tupi bows, which were larger than European ones, and it gives the Blackwood Archer its name. The Ibirapema Warrior carries the ibirapema, a wooden club painted and decorated with feathers that was used in close combat and in ritual killings of enemies. Much of this is known from Hans Staden, a German explorer held captive by the Tupinambá chief Cunhambebe in the 1550s.
turks: When Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, 70 guns battered the walls for eight weeks before 15,000 Janissaries led the final assault. The Turks play as gunpowder specialists to match, with the Janissary as a stronger Hand Cannoneer and an Artillery technology that gives Bombard Cannons, Bombard Towers and Cannon Galleons two more range.
vietnamese: In 1257, 1284 and 1287 the Tran dynasty drove back Kublai Khan's Mongol armies with clever use of terrain and guerrilla tactics. The same dynasty introduced paper money, and the Vietnamese Paper Money technology lets Lumberjacks earn gold as they work. A Vietnamese player also sees where every enemy starting Town Center stands from the first second of the game.
vikings: Dragon boats, named after the dragon heads carved on their bow and stern, carried Viking raiders across the sea, and in the west the raids began with the Danish attack on the island monastery of Lindisfarne. The Vikings were the first civilization in the game with two unique units, the Berserk and the Longship, and Bogsveigar gives both Longships and the Archer line +1 attack.
wei: Cao Cao fed his armies through tuntian, military farming colonies where soldiers worked the land, and the Wei technology of that name makes soldiers slowly produce food. His conquest of northern China also brought him strong cavalry: the Tiger Cavalry was his personal guard, and the Xianbei Raider recalls the Xianbei horsemen he absorbed into his army after subduing the northern tribes.
wu: Wu fire ships destroyed Cao Cao's larger fleet at the Battle of Red Cliffs, and the Red Cliffs Tactics technology lets Wu Demolition Ships and Fire Archers deal fire damage to ships and buildings. The Jian Swordsman echoes the kingdom's "dare to die" infantry, who once stripped off their armor to climb toward a Wei army: once badly hurt, he drops his shield, then hits harder and moves faster.
